explain.say: A battery does not store electricity like a tank of water; it stores chemicals that make electricity as they react. Every electron it sends out uses up a tiny bit of them.

faq.a: Not directly. It stores chemical energy, two materials that want to react. Only when a circuit is connected do they react and send electrons round.
asks: What is stored in a battery?

faq.q: Why do batteries go flat even when not used?
faq.a: Slow side reactions happen inside even with nothing connected, which is called self-discharge. Heat speeds them up, so batteries last longer kept somewhere cool.
asks: Do batteries run down in the drawer?

faq.q: How does recharging a battery work?
faq.a: A charger pushes current backwards through a rechargeable battery, driving the chemical reaction in reverse. That rebuilds the fresh chemicals, ready to react again.

faq.q: Why does a torch get dimmer as the battery runs down?
faq.a: As the chemicals are used up, the voltage drops and the battery's own resistance rises. Less push means less current through the bulb, so it glows more weakly.
asks: Why does a dying battery make things weaker?

faq.q: Why do batteries get warm when used hard?
faq.a: Every battery has some internal resistance. When a big current flows, part of the energy turns into heat inside it, so powerful devices make batteries warm.

facts: Batteries self-discharge faster when warm, so storing them somewhere cool makes them last longer.
Lithium-ion batteries can typically be recharged hundreds to a few thousand times before they wear out.
